books.title: Starship Troopers
books.author: Robert A. Heinlein
books.myReview:
The book starts with Johnnie being brainwashed into being a career soldier even though he doesn't want to.

Throughout his training he reflects upon radical ideas of militarism as if he doesn't belong in such a word. The text gives you subtle hints (nothing more) of how different this world is from the time the book was written. You even see predictions of things wrong with today's society. What I expected was for the protagonist (or any other character) to understand gradually that this isn't how things should be;or that there might be a better way. But, no.

The military works, the beatings are successfull without reoffence, Rico's thoughts and objections are silenced and he becomes a proper bootlicker for the army even before he learns about the eventual conscription of his father.

Their enemy is brutal and unforgiving, as far away as a thing can be from a human physically and culturally. The arachnids/bugs are ruthless creatures without individuality, willing to sacrifice themselves and their kind for the death of one human.

Also includes a very passionate discussion about why we should beat children more which I thought was pretty funny.

books.author: Osamu Dazai
books.myReview:
This books pulls you in, in a similar fashion to what I can only describe as the fucked up version of a siren.

It's a terrible feeling to find something, anything at all, in common with Yōzō. Wouldn't recommend reading if you are even the tiniest bit content in your life at the moment.

Also fuck Horiki whoever he is.

---

« Horiki at heart did not treat me like a full human being. He could only consider me as the living corpse of a would-be suicide, a person dead to shame, an idiot ghost. His friendship had no other purpose but to utilize me in whichever way would most further his own pleasures. This thought naturally did not make me very happy, but I realized after a moment that it was entirely to be expected that Horiki should take this view of me; that from long ago, even as a child, I seemed to lack the qualifications of a human being; and that, for all I knew, contempt, even from Horiki, might be entirely merited. »

---

« I suppose it would be no exaggeration to say that the world is composed entirely of unhappy people. But those people can fight their unhappiness with society fairly and squarely, and society for its part easily understands and sympathizes with such struggles. My unhappiness stemmed entirely from my own vices, and I had no way of fighting anybody. If I had ever attempted to voice anything in the nature of a protest, even a single mumbled word, the whole of society—and not only Flatfish—would undoubtedly have cried out flabbergasted, “Imagine the audacity of him talking like that!” Am I what they call an egoist? Or am I the opposite, a man of excessively weak spirit? I really don’t know myself, but since I seem in either case to be a mass of vices, I drop steadily, inevitably, into unhappiness, and I have no specific plan to stave off my descent. »

books.title: Lords of the North (The Saxon Stories, #3)
books.author: Bernard Cornwell
books.myReview:
Sorry, Ootred or whatever your name is. Aura-farming only takes you two books far.

The first two books are fine. Uthred's identity crisis in The Last Kingdom is compelling and his reluctant companionship with Alfred, however abandoned toward the end of The Pale Horseman, is interesting. This one feels like filler and I should have foreseen this when I saw that the series was 13 books long.

I found the series entertaining to listen to. The audiobook came to my aid when I was bored (Jonathan Keeble is quite good at his work) and the writing style is mostly enjoyable, but I was bored of listening any more of Uthred. I don't find the character interesting anymore and I don't think I will.

And it's funny how he mentions the weavers every single time he meets a "villain" and decides to let them go before they can cause him harm or accuse him of — or oppose him because of — things that he definitely is guilty of.

I'm fine with just reading the summary of the rest of the series, thanks, whatever.

I am eternally thankful, despite their many mistakes handling their IP's, that Netflix has made an adaptation of many different works that are just so damn good.

They caught my attention with Into the Night and Yakamoz S-245 (a.k.a Into the Deep), and eventually I read the original.

I love the world building, the subtle jumps from 1K to 10K and beyond (which expand the story without having to tell every single moment of the characters' experiences), the little details in this already very dense piece of art, the changes in the 'emotes' of the main character, they just click for me.

Dukaj is truly a master of his work, and as I plan on reading his other works I look forward to his adaptation of Frostpunk.

All that is gold does not glitter,
Not all those who wander are lost;
The old that is strong does not wither,
Deep roots are not reached by the frost.

From the ashes a fire shall be woken,
A light from the shadows shall spring;
Renewed shall be blade that was broken,
The crownless again shall be king.

If an earthquake levels a city, people all over the world will send emergency supplies. This is so fundamentally human that it's found in every culture without exception. Yes, there are assholes who just don't care, but they're massively outnumbered by the people who do.
